# OpenSSL

The general-purpose cryptography toolkit — a library that most of the internet links against, plus a
command-line front end that is the standard way to *do* PKI work by hand. Used in labs 06, 07 and 09
of [[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]], alongside GnuPG and Easy-RSA.

## The subcommands the labs exercise

| Area | Subcommand | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| RSA keys | `genrsa`, `rsa` | generate a private key; derive the public half |
| Modern keygen | `genpkey` | algorithm-agnostic key and parameter generation, including DH parameters |
| Digests & signing | `dgst` | hash, sign with a private key, verify with a public one |
| Key agreement | `pkeyutl -derive`, `pkeyparam`, `pkey` | Diffie–Hellman derivation and key inspection |
| Certificates | `req`, `x509`, `ca` (via Easy-RSA) | CSR generation, self-signing, CA operations |
| Packaging | `pkcs12` | bundle key and certificate into a `.p12` |

The sign/verify pair is the heart of lab 07: sign a file with the private key, verify with the public
one, then modify the file and verify again to watch it fail — see [[digital-signatures]]. Easy-RSA
wraps the same primitives into a CA whose certificates then feed OpenVPN in lab 09.

## Where it sits against CrypTool

[[cryptool]] shows you what a primitive *does*; OpenSSL makes you produce the artefacts. The commands
are text, so they are reviewable and repeatable — which is precisely what the GUI crypto labs cannot
leave behind. That is also why OpenSSL is where the repository's failures are most visible: a
screenshot of a working demo hides nothing, whereas a command that returns an error is recorded as an
error.

## Operational notes worth keeping

- **Generate the CSR where the private key lives.** The private key must never leave the subject's
  machine — the whole non-repudiation argument in [[public-key-infrastructure]] rests on it.
- **A `.p12` is a private-key container by definition.** This repository's `.gitignore` excludes
  `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.jks`, `*.keystore` and `id_rsa*` so the rule holds by default
  rather than by vigilance.
- **The natural terminal output of key generation prints the private key.** That single fact drove a
  documentation decision in this repo — see [[omit-rsa-private-key-screenshot]].
- **Verification failures are informative and distinguishable.** Verifying against the wrong key and
  omitting the signature argument fail differently, which is exactly why the lab's chosen illustration
  keeps the failed attempts above the successful one.
